newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman assures minority Serbs of protection.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman assures minority Serbs of protection.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman has urged Croatians to live peacefully with minority Serbs when the enclave of Eastern Slavonia is reintegrated with Croatia after regional elections next month.

His appeal, made on Tuesday in eastern Croatia on the edge of U.N.-administered Eastern Slavonia, was meant to reassure Western countries whose money will be needed for postwar reconstruction that the region faced no more ethnic conflict.

Tudjman's mere appearance for the occasion of a bridge opening linked to his party's election campaign was politically significant since he has been battling cancer which has markedly reduced his public activities.

The 74-year-old authoritarian nationalist leader, who led Croatia to independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, moved about normally. But his voice seemed softer than before and he looked somewhat drawn. His mane of silver hair has thinned.
Tudjman, watched by crowds of flag-waving Croats, laid the foundation stone of a bridge across the Drava River at Belisce which will link the town with nearby Eastern Slavonia.
He called on Croats, especially 80,000 war refugees who will move back to their homes in Eastern Slavonia after reintegration, to accept Serbs as their neighbours.
"Those who organised the war against Croatia (after declaration of independence in 1991) are probably no longer here, or will not remain here," he told the crowd.
"Those who do stay can rest assured that they will be protected by the Croatian authorities, that they will be able to live here in peace, with all civil, human, and ethnic rights," Tudjman said.
"(Displaced Croats) should show their wisdom and be ready to extend their hand to Serbs not involved in war crimes."

Under international pressure, Zagreb has promised extensive minority rights to Serbs in the enclave and whittled a once long and poorly substantiated list of suspected Serb war criminals down to 150 names of indictees.
Many local Serbs doubt whether the central government's guarantees will be honoured once U.N. authorities leave and also fear violent retribution from returning Croats.

But more than 60,000 of 120,000-odd Serbs in the area have obtained Croatian citizenship papers in a sign that most will stay to test Zagreb's commitments and not flee to nearby Serbia, at least in the beginning.

Local Serbs have also been heartened by a budding accord between Croatia and Serbian-led Yugoslavia under which they would be entitled to dual citizenship. This would also apply to minority Croats living in Yugoslavia.
